studies.title: Mindfulness courses genuinely lower levels of the stress hormone cortisol
studies.ns_score_reason: first meta-analysis to pin a physiological, not just self-reported, effect on mindfulness training; heterogeneity and small effect size hold it back.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Researchers pooled 39 trials of mindfulness-based stress reduction (MBSR) — the standardized 8-week program — that measured cortisol before and after and controlled for the time of day samples were taken, covering 2,059 participants. MBSR lowered cortisol relative to controls (g = −0.38), with a bigger drop against inactive controls (g = −0.42) than active ones (g = −0.29), and the within-group effect appeared only in randomized trials, not uncontrolled ones.
studies.why_it_matters: Mindfulness research has long been dogged by the criticism that its benefits are self-reported and expectation-driven; this is the strongest pooled evidence yet that an eight-week course shifts a hard biological marker of stress, though the effect is modest.
studies.pitch_angle: Everyone who has been told to "just breathe" suspects mindfulness is placebo with a mat. Open on someone halfway through week four of an MBSR course, then reveal that the cortisol data hold up — but only in properly controlled trials, and by less than the wellness industry implies. Call Blair Johnson at the University of Connecticut, who led the meta-analysis, and ask what the unexplained heterogeneity means.
studies.wider_angle: For a health or business outlet: the workplace wellness question. Employers are buying mindfulness apps by the seat; this analysis suggests the full eight-week, in-person program has measurable physiology behind it, while the app-sized doses tested against active controls do much less. A piece on what dose of mindfulness is actually evidenced.
studies.caveats: Substantial unexplained heterogeneity between studies; cortisol is a noisy biomarker; no data on whether cortisol changes translate into health outcomes; publication bias not fully excluded.

studies.title: People who put things off rate their own health as worse — and stress explains part of it
studies.ns_score_reason: big multi-sample dataset on an everyday trait almost everyone recognizes in themselves; cross-sectional design limits how far it can be pushed.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Fuschia Sirois and a colleague meta-analyzed 36 cross-sectional samples totaling 8,603 people who reported trait procrastination and rated their current and future health. Chronic procrastinators rated their health as worse (average r = .21) and their future health as somewhat worse (r = .13); controlling for perceived stress shrank but did not eliminate the link to current health, and wiped out the link to future health entirely. Procrastinators nonetheless expected their health to improve slightly over the next decade.
studies.why_it_matters: It reframes procrastination as a stress-generating trait with body-wide consequences rather than a time-management quirk — and hints that the same optimism that lets people delay a task also lets them assume their health will sort itself out later.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the mismatch: procrastinators feel unhealthy now but confidently expect to feel better in 10 years — the same "future me will handle it" logic that got them there. Open on a reader delaying a doctor's appointment. Call Fuschia Sirois at Durham University, who has built the procrastination–health model over two decades.
studies.wider_angle: A feature for a general-interest magazine on the psychology of deferred consequences — why the brain treats future selves as strangers, spanning pensions, climate inaction and unfilled prescriptions, with procrastination research as the empirical spine.
studies.caveats: All samples cross-sectional — cannot establish causation; outcomes entirely self-reported, including health status; "future health" measured as expectation, not outcome; samples skew toward students and convenience recruitment.

studies.title: Newborn babies can already hear when their own language is spoken with a foreign rhythm
studies.ns_score_reason: overturns a textbook claim about what newborns can hear; clean design, but modest N and a single language pairing.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Forty-four Czech newborns listened to naturally spoken, well-formed Czech sentences delivered either with native Czech rhythm or with a foreign-accented rhythm (lengthened foot-initial syllables) while their brain hemodynamics were recorded. Their brains responded more strongly to the foreign-rhythm version, with the difference strongest in the right hemisphere.
studies.why_it_matters: Standard theory holds that at birth infants can only tell apart languages from broadly different rhythm classes — this shows they pick up fine-grained timing differences within their own language, presumably learned in the womb.
studies.pitch_angle: Open in a maternity ward: a baby hours old, hearing its mother tongue spoken by someone with an accent, and reacting. The hook is that prenatal listening is far more detailed than assumed — newborns aren't sorting languages into crude rhythm buckets, they're tracking syllable timing. Call Kateřina Chládková at Charles University in Prague.
studies.wider_angle: For a parenting or education outlet: what fetuses actually learn in the third trimester, and what that means for bilingual households, premature babies in noisy NICUs, and the marketing claims made for prenatal audio products.
studies.caveats: N = 44, single center; one language and one accent manipulation; hemodynamic response tells you the brain distinguished the sounds, not what the baby "understood"; population may not generalize to other rhythm classes.

studies.title: The evidence that therapy helps bullying victims largely vanishes once publication bias is corrected
studies.ns_score_reason: a genuinely deflating correction to an accepted literature; the story is about method, which makes it a slightly harder sell.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (1 hits)
studies.the_study: A team at Ghent University pooled 23 studies of individual cognitive behavioral therapy (n = 15) and imagery-based interventions (n = 8) for people with psychological problems related to bullying. Raw effects looked healthy — internalizing symptoms fell with g = 0.72 — but after adjusting for publication bias the pre-post effect dropped to g = 0.26 and lost statistical significance. Curiously, the adjusted effect on self-perception and coping went the other way, rising to g = 0.98, and the follow-up effect on internalizing symptoms remained significant but small (g = 0.37).
studies.why_it_matters: Schools and services routinely refer bullied children to CBT; this suggests the symptom-reduction evidence base is thinner than headline numbers imply, while the case for improving how victims see and manage themselves may be stronger than assumed.
studies.pitch_angle: The surprise is directional: correcting for publication bias didn't just shrink the effect, it swapped which outcome looks best. Open on a bullied 13-year-old referred for six sessions of CBT and ask what those sessions realistically deliver. Call Ernst Koster's group at Ghent University.
studies.wider_angle: For a specialist or education outlet: an investigation into how anti-bullying interventions get commissioned in schools, and how far procurement decisions lean on unadjusted meta-analytic effect sizes.
studies.caveats: Only 23 heterogeneous studies (I² = 68–98%); many were small and at risk of bias; adjusted estimates are model-dependent; pooled across ages and intervention formats.

studies.title: Brain stimulation for PTSD works on questionnaires but not on clinician interviews
studies.ns_score_reason: a clean split between self-report and blinded-rater outcomes is exactly the kind of red flag readers should know about; the negative framing limits reach.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: A Spanish team systematically reviewed and meta-analyzed randomized controlled trials of repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) for PTSD, with 16 trials and 786 participants in the main sham-controlled comparison. Self-reported PTSD symptoms improved substantially compared with sham, but interview-based outcomes did not reach significance, heterogeneity was large, prediction intervals were wide, and evidence beyond the treatment period was sparse. Adverse events were mild.
studies.why_it_matters: rTMS is being marketed and rolled out for trauma; this analysis suggests the apparent benefit rides largely on how symptoms are measured, and the overall certainty of the evidence is low to very low.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the discrepancy — patients say they feel better, trained assessors can't detect it. That gap is the story, and it applies far beyond rTMS. Open on a veteran paying out of pocket for a course of stimulation. Call Wenceslao Peñate-Castro at the University of La Laguna.
studies.wider_angle: For a health-policy or investigative outlet: the private neuromodulation clinic market, what it claims for PTSD, and what regulators require as proof before a device-based treatment can be advertised.
studies.caveats: Secondary analysis of published trials; substantial between-study heterogeneity; protocols, coil placement and dosing varied widely; short follow-up in most trials; certainty of evidence rated low or very low by the authors.

studies.title: Men recover from PTSD in about a decade — for women it takes twice as long
studies.journal: Australian & New Zealand Journal of Psychiatry
studies.ns_score_reason: nationally representative, diagnostic-interview data with a striking sex asymmetry in recovery time; the design is descriptive epidemiology.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Using diagnostic interviews with 15,893 people in Australia's 2020–2022 National Study of Mental Health and Wellbeing, researchers estimated lifetime PTSD prevalence at 7.1% and projected lifetime risk at 9.6%. Women were more than twice as likely to be diagnosed, and although about 63% of people eventually remit, three quarters of men reached remission within 10 years versus 20 years for women. Prevalence had not changed since the 2007 survey.
studies.why_it_matters: It quantifies something clinicians suspect but rarely see in national data — that PTSD is not just more common in women but far more persistent — and it shows that despite two decades of trauma awareness, population prevalence hasn't budged.
studies.pitch_angle: The headline number is time: a decade of difference in how long PTSD lasts, depending on sex. Open on the flat prevalence line between 2007 and 2022 — trauma treatment has improved, so why hasn't the population picture? Call Katherine Mills at the Matilda Centre, University of Sydney.
studies.wider_angle: For a specialist psychiatry or public-health outlet: PTSD as a multisystem condition. The same survey ties PTSD to doubled odds of asthma and raised odds of diabetes and sedative use disorder — a piece on why trauma clinics may need physicians in the room.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional survey with retrospective age-of-onset and remission reporting; DSM-IV criteria; Australian population may not generalize; remission estimates rest on recall.

studies.title: On days you procrastinate, tomorrow's stress rises — and stress feeds back into attention problems
studies.ns_score_reason: 28 days of intensive daily data resolving the direction of a chicken-and-egg question; student sample and self-report cap it.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: A total of 187 undergraduates (mean age 19.7; 78% women) reported ADHD symptoms and perceived stress daily for 28 days, and the researchers modeled temporal, contemporaneous and between-person networks. Days with more concentration difficulty and procrastination were followed by higher perceived stress the next day; days with more perceived stress — especially feeling a lack of control — were followed by more ADHD symptoms the next day.
studies.why_it_matters: It shows a genuinely bidirectional, day-scale loop between attentional symptoms and stress, and identifies which specific symptoms (procrastination, restlessness, loss of control) sit at the hinge points — plausible targets for very short, in-the-moment interventions.
studies.pitch_angle: ADHD is described as a lifelong trait, but these data show it fluctuating from Tuesday to Wednesday in step with stress. Open on a student in an exam period watching the loop tighten. Call Patrick Goh at the University of Hawai'i at Mānoa, and ask whether the same dynamics hold in diagnosed adults.
studies.wider_angle: For a technology or higher-education outlet: the rise of "micro-interventions" delivered by phone at the moment a symptom spikes, and whether ecological momentary assessment can move from measurement tool to treatment.
studies.caveats: Non-clinical student sample, not a diagnosed ADHD cohort; all measures self-reported; N = 187 with heavy female skew; network models are correlational and cannot establish causation.

studies.title: Difficulty naming your own emotions seems to protect fragile narcissists from burnout
studies.ns_score_reason: a genuinely odd buffering effect in a large clinical sample; retrospective chart data and a single Swiss clinic limit it.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Researchers analyzed routinely collected psychometric data from 1,239 adults treated as inpatients for stress-related disorders at a Swiss clinic between 2018 and 2024. Burnout was predicted by alexithymia (difficulty identifying and describing feelings), effort–reward imbalance at work, and overcommitment. Unexpectedly, the alexithymia × narcissistic vulnerability interaction was significant and negative: at high levels of alexithymia, the effect of narcissistic vulnerability on burnout was attenuated.
studies.why_it_matters: Emotional awareness is usually cast as protective; here, not being in touch with your feelings appears to blunt the burnout cost of a fragile ego — a wrinkle for interventions that assume more emotional insight is always better.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the paradox: in a clinic full of burned-out professionals, the ones least able to name what they feel were partly insulated from the damage of a fragile self-image. Open on an inpatient program for exhausted managers. Call Katharina Ledermann at University Hospital Zurich, and press her on whether this is protection or just under-reporting.
studies.wider_angle: For a business or work-culture outlet: burnout is being medicalized as a personality problem while effort–reward imbalance remains the single strongest predictor in this dataset — a piece on the quiet shift of responsibility from employer to employee.
studies.caveats: Retrospective observational study, single center, no control group; cannot establish causation; burnout and alexithymia both self-reported, raising the possibility that alexithymia suppresses symptom reporting rather than symptoms; inpatient sample not representative of working population.

studies.title: Loneliness predicts later suicidal thoughts even after accounting for depression and anxiety
studies.ns_score_reason: large longitudinal population sample with strong statistical controls; the direction of the finding is not surprising.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: A German team surveyed 4,277 people aged 18–89 at two time points and tested whether baseline loneliness predicted later suicidal ideation or behavior. Across all four age bands, loneliness remained a significant predictor after controlling for gender, size of social circle, depression, anxiety, stress, and prior lifetime suicidality — the models explained 25–39% of the variance.
studies.why_it_matters: Loneliness is usually treated as a symptom of depression; these data indicate it carries independent prospective risk, and that the size of someone's social network does not capture it.
studies.pitch_angle: The counterintuitive detail is that how many people you know is not what matters — loneliness predicted risk even with social circle size controlled. Open on the gap between a full contacts list and an empty evening. Call Tobias Teismann at Ruhr-Universität Bochum. Frame as risk assessment research, not a treatment claim.
studies.wider_angle: For a policy or general-interest outlet: whether national loneliness strategies (UK, Japan, Germany) are measuring the right thing, given that connection quality rather than contact frequency is what tracks with harm.
studies.caveats: Observational, two-wave design — cannot establish causation; online convenience panel; all measures self-reported; suicidal ideation and behavior combined into a single outcome.

studies.title: Living with long-term stress may blunt, not amplify, the daily link between hassles and low mood
studies.ns_score_reason: result runs directly opposite the authors' hypothesis, which is interesting; N = 61 keeps it a line of enquiry rather than a finding.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Sixty-one young men who have sex with men living with HIV, recruited at three US Adolescent Trials Network sites, reported daily stressors and mood by phone for 66 days, with chronic HIV-related stressors measured at baseline. Daily stressors predicted both a higher level and greater day-to-day swing in depressed mood — but among participants carrying more chronic HIV stressors, those daily associations were weaker, not stronger.
studies.why_it_matters: It challenges the intuitive "stress sensitization" model in which chronic adversity leaves people more reactive to everyday knocks, raising the possibility of either adaptive toughening or a blunted stress response.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the reversal: the researchers expected chronic stress to make bad days worse, and found the opposite. Open on one participant's 66 days of phone diaries. Call Patrick Wilson's lab at UCLA and ask which explanation they favor — resilience or physiological dysregulation.
studies.wider_angle: For a specialist health outlet: what intensive longitudinal phone data is revealing about living with HIV as a chronic condition in your twenties, and why mood variability rather than average mood may matter most for treatment adherence.
studies.caveats: Small N (61), no control group, observational; highly specific population that will not generalize; all mood and stress measures self-reported; the attenuation effect could reflect floor or ceiling effects in reporting.

studies.title: Erratic dinner times are linked to more depressive symptoms — breakfast and lunch aren't
studies.ns_score_reason: a specific, testable meal-timing signal that readers can picture; cross-sectional convenience sample and a null on the categorical analysis temper it.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: Researchers in Tehran assessed 450 healthy adults aged 20–59 using three non-consecutive 24-hour dietary recalls, calculating composite phase deviation scores for how variable each person's breakfast, lunch and dinner timing was. Adjusting for sleep quality, chronotype, physical activity and demographics, dinner timing irregularity was associated with higher depressive symptom scores (B = 1.08), while breakfast and lunch irregularity showed nothing, and there were no associations with anxiety or stress.
studies.why_it_matters: It points to the evening meal specifically as the circadian anchor that may matter for mood — a much more actionable hypothesis than "eat regularly" — but only a trial can tell whether fixing dinner time does anything.
studies.pitch_angle: Of three daily meals, only one tracked with depressive symptoms. Open on a shift worker or a parent whose dinner lands anywhere between 6pm and 11pm, then explain why the evening meal may be the body clock's most important non-light cue. Call Sakineh Shab-Bidar at Tehran University of Medical Sciences. Do not imply that changing dinner time treats depression.
studies.wider_angle: For a nutrition or lifestyle outlet: the emerging science of chrononutrition — when you eat versus what you eat — and why time-restricted eating trials have so far focused on metabolism and ignored mood.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional — cannot establish direction (low mood may itself disorganize eating); convenience sampling; self-reported symptoms and dietary recall; the categorical tertile analysis was null, with the finding surviving only in continuous models; single country.

studies.title: Children born preterm run hot: raised heart rate at five, but normal stress regulation
studies.ns_score_reason: cleanly separates "aroused" from "dysregulated," which reframes a common assumption; modest sample and one age point.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: Seventy preterm-born children aged 5.5 years and 32 matched full-term controls had heart rate and heart rate variability recorded at rest and during structured social interactions with their mother and with a stranger, including eye contact, conversation and triadic play. Preterm children showed more social difficulties and internalizing problems and consistently higher heart rate across all conditions — but their heart rate variability tracked social context in exactly the same way as full-term peers, with conversation the most physiologically demanding task for both groups.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests prematurity's autonomic legacy is elevated baseline arousal rather than a broken regulatory system, which changes what any intervention should be aiming at.
studies.pitch_angle: The finding is a distinction people rarely make: being permanently on edge is not the same as being unable to calm down. Open on a five-year-old meeting a stranger, heart racing but regulating normally. Call Bart Boets at KU Leuven. Also worth noting: talking to someone stressed both groups more than making eye contact did.
studies.wider_angle: For a parenting or neonatology outlet: what follow-up care for preterm children currently monitors (motor and cognitive milestones) versus what these data suggest it should also track (arousal and social-emotional function into school age).
studies.caveats: Small N by cohort standards (70 vs 32), single center, 98% White sample so limited generalizability; cross-sectional at one age; parent-reported social difficulties.

studies.title: When childhood abuse happens may matter more than how much of it there was
studies.ns_score_reason: the null on cumulative severity is the interesting part; small N and exploratory machine-learning approach limit confidence.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Researchers measured blood markers of oxidative stress in 116 young adults (mean age 26.3) who had spent time in residential care as children, and mapped them against detailed year-by-year histories of maltreatment type and timing. Abuse during adolescence was associated with higher glutathione reductase and neglect with lower levels; neglect at ages 8 and 12 stood out for the GPx/GRed ratio. Overall severity, multiplicity and total duration of maltreatment showed no association with any marker.
studies.why_it_matters: Adversity research overwhelmingly uses cumulative "how many, how bad" scores; this suggests those totals may obscure biologically specific windows in which particular kinds of harm register.
studies.pitch_angle: The surprise is a null: the more-is-worse ACE score model found nothing here, while narrow age windows did. Open on the difference between a childhood tallied as a score and one reconstructed year by year. Call Vera Clemens at University Hospital Ulm or David Bürgin in Basel. Frame strictly as biomarker association, not risk prediction.
studies.wider_angle: For a specialist or long-read outlet: the growing challenge to the ACE score, the single most influential instrument in child trauma policy, and what a timing-sensitive replacement would look like in practice.
studies.caveats: Small N (116) with only 30.5% women; observational and cross-sectional; retrospective recall of childhood timing; exploratory random-forest analysis with many predictors; care-experienced population is not representative; oxidative stress markers have uncertain clinical meaning.

studies.title: Children whose parents and coaches both push winning report the most stress — and the least fun
studies.ns_score_reason: first study to profile parent and coach climates together rather than separately, with a relatable result; self-report and cross-sectional.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: A total of 347 adolescent athletes (65% female, mean age 12.5) rated the motivational climates created by their parents and their coaches, along with their own goal orientations, enjoyment and stress. Latent profile analysis identified five combined climate profiles. Athletes in predominantly mastery-focused profiles reported high enjoyment and low stress; those in performance-leaning profiles reported the reverse; and, notably, athletes getting both mastery and performance messaging from both adults reported adaptive *and* maladaptive outcomes simultaneously.
studies.why_it_matters: It shows that parents and coaches don't cancel each other out — mixed messages from both sides produce a mixed psychological profile, not a neutral one.
studies.pitch_angle: Open on the touchline: a coach shouting about effort and a parent shouting about the scoreboard. The new finding is what happens when a child gets both messages at once — they get the enjoyment and the stress. Call Sarah Fuller and Erin Moore at East Carolina University.
studies.wider_angle: For a sports or parenting outlet: youth sport dropout rates around ages 12–14, and whether the climate a child is embedded in — rather than talent or injury — is the real predictor of who quits.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional and entirely self-reported by the athletes; single-country sample; profiles are descriptive and cannot establish that climate causes stress; N = 347 spread across five profiles leaves some groups small.

studies.title: Growing up in a war zone changes which brain circuits track a child's attachment style
studies.ns_score_reason: timely and methodologically careful about what it doesn't show; modest N and uncorrected secondary results.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Seventy-nine children in Israel — 42 with war-related exposure, 37 without — underwent resting-state fMRI plus assessments of attachment characteristics and parent-reported executive function. The groups did not differ in attachment or, after adjustment, in executive function. But the brain–behavior coupling diverged: in war-exposed children, attachment anxiety and avoidance tracked reduced cingulate–amygdala connectivity, whereas in unexposed children the same traits tracked reduced amygdala–hippocampal connectivity.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests extreme environmental unpredictability doesn't necessarily produce a uniformly "damaged" brain or personality, but rewires which circuits carry a given psychological trait — a subtler model of adversity than group-difference studies deliver.
studies.pitch_angle: The result nobody expects: war-exposed and unexposed children looked the same on attachment questionnaires and, after adjustment, on executive function. The difference was only visible in which circuits the traits mapped onto. Call Tzipi Horowitz-Kraus at the Technion. Emphasize preliminary status.
studies.wider_angle: For a foreign-affairs or long-form outlet: the science of measuring war's effect on children, and why the standard toolkit — symptom checklists, group comparisons — may systematically miss what conflict actually does to developing brains.
studies.caveats: Observational, cross-sectional, N = 79; some key network results did not survive correction for multiple comparisons and the authors flag them as tentative; parent-reported executive function; exposure index structured but unvalidated; no longitudinal follow-up.

studies.title: The largest genetic map yet of everyday moodiness and impulsivity points to two different brain regions
studies.ns_score_reason: enormous sample and a clean anatomical dissociation; genomic-SEM stories are hard to make vivid for general readers.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Using genomic structural equation modeling across 13 genome-wide association studies of non-clinical population traits (samples of 64,000 to 1.2 million), researchers built two-factor models of externalizing (impulsive, outward-directed) and internalizing (anxious, inward-directed) behavior. They found 184 genome-wide significant loci for externalizing and 31 for internalizing, plus 70 novel genes. Single-cell expression pointed to hippocampal CA4 neurons for externalizing and amygdalar excitatory neurons for internalizing, and internalizing polygenic scores predicted emotional well-being in an independent cohort of 4,565 people.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests the two broadest dimensions of human temperament have partly distinct cellular addresses in the brain, and that the genetics of ordinary personality variation shade continuously into psychiatric diagnoses rather than being separate.
studies.pitch_angle: Two of the oldest categories in psychology — acting out versus turning inward — turn out to point at two different neuron populations. Open on the continuum question: the same variants that make someone restless in the general population are the ones enriched in ADHD and substance-use disorder. Call Barbara Franke at Radboud University Medical Center.
studies.wider_angle: For a specialist genetics outlet: the rise of genomic structural equation modeling and transdiagnostic psychiatry, and what it means for a diagnostic system built on discrete categories.
studies.caveats: Predominantly European-ancestry GWAS data — will not generalize globally; effect sizes at the individual level are tiny and non-predictive; enrichment analyses are inferential, not direct measurements of brain tissue; industry-adjacent disclosure (BF has received speaking fees and travel support from Medice).

studies.title: Older men with more mentally rich lifestyles report less stress — but more loneliness
studies.ns_score_reason: the paradox is genuinely odd, but the study is explicitly exploratory with N = 80 and sex-split results the authors themselves distrust.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Eighty independently living Spanish adults aged 65–101 completed measures of cognitive reserve (built from educational, occupational and leisure engagement), stress, anxiety, loneliness and life satisfaction, plus memory-span and spatial-cueing attention tasks. Among men only, higher cognitive reserve scores were associated with both lower perceived stress and greater reported loneliness. Cognitive reserve related to some attention measures but not to memory span.
studies.why_it_matters: Not much yet — but it raises an awkward question for the "stay mentally active" prescription: some of the activities that build reserve are solitary, and the trade-off with social connection has barely been examined.
studies.pitch_angle: The uncomfortable possibility is that a lifetime of reading, studying and solitary hobbies buys cognitive resilience at a social cost — at least for men. Open on a retired engineer with a full bookshelf and a quiet phone. Call Mikhail Ordin at the University of the Basque Country, and be upfront that this is hypothesis-generating.
studies.wider_angle: For a general-interest or aging outlet: how "cognitive reserve" became a consumer product — brain-training apps, adult education, puzzle subscriptions — and how thin the evidence for the leisure component of the construct actually is.
studies.caveats: Small N (80), cross-sectional, exploratory with no pre-registration; sex-specific findings from subgroups of roughly 33 men and 47 women and explicitly flagged by the authors as needing caution; self-reported stress and loneliness; Spanish community sample only.

studies.title: A key theory of what drives suicidal thinking holds up in the US but not in the UK
studies.ns_score_reason: an honest cross-national non-replication of a moderation effect, which is useful but technical; the main effects replicate fine.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Testing the Integrated Motivational-Volitional model of suicide, researchers examined whether sexual and gender minority (SGM) status changes the relationship between feelings of defeat and entrapment and suicidal thoughts, across a US college sample (n = 865) and a UK adult community sample (n = 734). Defeat and entrapment predicted suicidal ideation in both samples and SGM participants reported more lifetime ideation in both. But the moderation effect — entrapment mattering more for SGM people — appeared only in the US students and did not replicate in the UK adults.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests the core psychological mechanism is universal while the identity-specific amplification is context-dependent, which matters for whether prevention programs can be exported wholesale between countries.
studies.pitch_angle: Two samples, one theory, two different answers about whether minority stress amplifies entrapment. Open on the question of whether a US college campus and a UK community sample are even measuring the same social experience. Call Rory O'Connor at the University of Glasgow, who developed the IMV model.
studies.wider_angle: For a science-methods or specialist outlet: the replication problem in moderation analyses specifically — interaction effects are underpowered almost everywhere in psychology, and this study is a clean worked example.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional, self-reported; samples differ in both country and life stage (students versus community adults), confounding the comparison; SGM defined broadly, collapsing very different groups; suicidal ideation measured retrospectively.

studies.title: Nonbinary people describe the current political climate in the language of trauma and bereavement
studies.ns_score_reason: genuinely novel framing of political events as a trauma exposure, in a flagship journal; qualitative design and no quantitative outcomes cap it.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Using mixed methods, researchers thematically analyzed open-text survey responses from nonbinary people about the impact of the current US sociopolitical climate, then tested whether themes differed by race, gender expression and geography. Four themes emerged — trauma and stress from the climate, grief over lost self and lost connection to society, emotional consequences, and resistance. Rural participants more often described a loss of authenticity; gender-nonconforming participants more often described a loss of possible future.
studies.why_it_matters: It makes the case that sustained legislative hostility functions psychologically like a chronic trauma exposure rather than as ordinary political stress — a framing with direct implications for how clinicians assess and code such distress.
studies.pitch_angle: The most striking finding is grammatical: participants describe a *future* they have lost, not only a present they endure — anticipatory grief as a stress exposure. Open on a rural nonbinary participant describing dressing differently to leave the house. Call Em Matsuno at Arizona State University.
studies.wider_angle: For a policy or health-affairs outlet: the emerging concept of "sociopolitical trauma" and whether psychology's diagnostic frameworks, built around discrete threatening events, can accommodate a slow-moving legislative environment.
studies.caveats: Qualitative write-in responses with no control group or baseline; self-selected survey sample, likely skewed toward the most affected; chi-square subgroup comparisons on theme endorsement are exploratory; US-specific and time-bound; no clinical outcome measures.

citation_table.journal: Australian & New Zealand Journal of Psychiatry

trends_raw:
**Convergent findings**
- Loneliness keeps coming apart from its usual proxies. Last run's "Lonely brains respond less to their own heartbeat" (PMID 42456921) found loneliness tracked appraisal of bodily signals, not raw detection accuracy; this run's "Loneliness predicts later suicidal thoughts even after accounting for depression and anxiety" (PMID 42642073) finds it predicts risk independently of depression, anxiety, stress *and* the size of someone's social circle. Two different methods, same message: loneliness is not a headcount and not just a depressive symptom.
- Self-report versus harder measurement continues to split results. Previously, actigraphy revealed a delayed sleep benefit invisible to questionnaires in PTSD treatment (PMID 42660579) and post-concussion checklists behaved like distress scales (PMID 42173054). This run, "Brain stimulation for PTSD works on questionnaires but not on clinician interviews" (PMID 42680058) shows the same fault line inside a single meta-analysis, while "Mindfulness courses genuinely lower levels of the stress hormone cortisol" (PMID 42691284) is the mirror image — a physiological outcome finally backing what was previously only self-reported.
- Unbundling composite constructs keeps changing the answer. Last run it was acculturation stress splitting into two opposite-signed pressures (PMID 42682243); this run it is cumulative maltreatment scores yielding nothing while narrow age windows do ("When childhood abuse happens may matter more than how much of it there was", PMID 42683544), and meal-timing irregularity mattering only at dinner (PMID 42624213).

**Advances**
- Intensive daily sampling moves from documenting associations to resolving direction. The previous digest used daily diaries to show perfectionism damages sleep via stress (PMID 41989986) and hourly sensors to break the stress–inactivity link (PMID 42612762). This run's "On days you procrastinate, tomorrow's stress rises" (PMID 42695429) uses 28 days of network modeling to pin a bidirectional day-scale loop, and "Living with long-term stress may blunt, not amplify, the daily link between hassles and low mood" (PMID 42595230) uses 66 days to test — and reverse — the stress sensitization model.
- PTSD moves from trial to population scale. Last run gave two treatment studies (PMIDs 42660579, 42635370); "Men recover from PTSD in about a decade — for women it takes twice as long" (PMID 42303590) supplies the epidemiological backdrop showing flat prevalence across 15 years despite those treatment advances.
- The procrastination thread now has two independent legs: trait-level health perceptions mediated by stress (PMID 42569817) and day-level procrastination predicting next-day stress (PMID 42695429).

**Counterpoints**
- Infant speech rhythm findings now pull against each other. The previous digest's three-language infant EEG study (PMID 42621832) concluded that the syllable is a universal default and language-specific rhythmic tuning arrives late; this run's Czech newborns (PMID 42464912) discriminate foreign-accented timing within their native language hours after birth. Worth reporting as a live disagreement about how early prenatal listening shapes perception.
- Evidence-base deflation continues but is no longer uniformly negative. Where last run offered a clean double null (PMID 41680576), this run's bullying-therapy correction (PMID 42658011) shows publication-bias adjustment *swapping* which outcome looks strongest, and the IMV replication (PMID 42683538) shows main effects holding while only the moderation fails.

**New themes**
- Political and wartime environments treated as stress exposures in their own right: "Growing up in a war zone changes which brain circuits track a child's attachment style" (PMID 42607893) and "Nonbinary people describe the current political climate in the language of trauma and bereavement" (PMID 42658624). Nothing comparable in the previous digest beyond the Ukraine treatment study.
- Genetics enters the topic for the first time with the externalizing/internalizing genomic-SEM map (PMID 42679763).
feature_pitch_raw:
**The pattern:** Several studies here find that *totals* — the summed adversity score, the group average, the composite exposure — hide the signal, while timing, configuration and which specific component you look at carry it. Oxidative stress markers in care-experienced adults tracked abuse at particular ages while overall severity, multiplicity and duration showed nothing (PMID 42683544); depressive symptoms tracked dinner-time irregularity but not breakfast or lunch (PMID 42624213); war-exposed and unexposed children were indistinguishable on attachment and executive-function scores yet differed in which circuits those traits mapped onto (PMID 42607893); preterm five-year-olds showed elevated baseline arousal but entirely normal context-tracking regulation (PMID 42693548); and young athletes getting mastery messages from one adult and performance messages from another ended up with high enjoyment *and* high stress rather than a neutral average (PMID 42419608).

**Why pitch this now:** The ACE score and its cousins — cumulative exposure indices, group-difference designs, composite symptom checklists — underpin trauma screening in pediatrics, schools and child protection, and this is a cluster of papers, arriving in the same month, showing those instruments returning nulls where finer-grained reconstructions return structure. The methods that make the alternative possible (year-by-year maltreatment histories, daily sampling, connectivity mapping) have only recently become routine.

**Angle:** A reported feature on the shift from dose to pattern in adversity research — what a childhood looks like when it is reconstructed year by year instead of scored out of ten, who is trying to build a timing-sensitive replacement, and what would have to change in screening practice if they succeeded. For general science readers plus the clinicians, teachers and social workers who currently fill in these forms.

**Potential headlines:**
- Timing of childhood abuse showed up in the blood; the total amount did not
- The adversity score that keeps finding nothing
- Your childhood, added up wrong

**Potential outlets:**
- **New Scientist Features** — the Mind desk can carry a construct-under-revision piece assembled from several current papers, with the biomarker and brain-imaging strands giving it hard edges.
- **Undark** — consistently strong on instruments that outrun their evidence base, and the ACE score's journey from research tool to policy fixture is exactly that story.
- **STAT** — the clinical-screening angle: ACE questionnaires are already embedded in pediatric practice in parts of the US, and STAT covers the gap between screening enthusiasm and validation.
- **Knowable Magazine** — well suited to a piece explaining why a whole field is rethinking how it quantifies exposure, with room for the developmental and psychophysiology detail.

fact_check.raw:
# Fact-Check Report: New Scientist Story Ideas — Stress — September 2026
**Checked:** 2026-09-06 | **Studies reviewed:** 19
**Publication:** New Scientist | **Section:** New Scientist Mind

---

# Fact-Check Report — New Scientist Mind digest, run date 2026-09-06

---

### Study 1: Mindfulness courses genuinely lower levels of the stress hormone cortisol
**PMID:** 42691284 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

Core numbers all check out: 39 studies, 2,059 participants, between-group g = −0.38, inactive controls g = −0.42, active controls g = −0.29, within-group effect present in RCTs (g = −0.37) but not uncontrolled studies (g = −0.06). Author and institution correct.

**Issue A. "8-week" program length not in abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "39 trials of mindfulness-based stress reduction (MBSR) — the standardized 8-week program"
- **Abstract says:** "Mindfulness-based stress reduction (MBSR), a standardized multiweek program"
- **Problem:** The abstract never specifies eight weeks. MBSR conventionally runs eight weeks, but the pooled trials are described only as "multiweek," and the "Why it matters" and wider angle both lean on the eight-week figure. Unverifiable from abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "39 trials of mindfulness-based stress reduction (MBSR) — the standardised multiweek programme (conventionally eight weeks)"

**Issue B. Active controls recast as "app-sized doses"** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "this analysis suggests the full eight-week, in-person program has measurable physiology behind it, while the app-sized doses tested against active controls do much less."
- **Abstract says:** "MBSR had larger reductions compared with inactive controls (k = 23, g = −0.42) and smaller reductions compared with active controls (k = 11, g = −0.29)."
- **Problem:** The active/inactive contrast is about what the *comparison* condition was, not about the dose of mindfulness delivered to the intervention arm. Every arm analyzed was MBSR. Nothing in the abstract tests app-delivered or abbreviated mindfulness, so the wider angle's dose–response hook is not supported by the data.
- **Suggested fix:** "this analysis suggests the full MBSR programme has measurable physiology behind it, though the effect shrinks when it is compared against an active control rather than a waitlist — a reminder that part of the benefit may be non-specific. It says nothing directly about app-delivered mindfulness, which was not tested."

**NS fit 7/10:** Defensible — pooled RCT evidence on an objective biomarker.

---

### Study 2: People who put things off rate their own health as worse — and stress explains part of it
**PMID:** 42569817 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

36 samples, N = 8,603, r = .21 and r = .13, semi-partial effects reduced-but-significant for SRH and non-significant for future SRH, and the slight expected improvement over 10 years all match. Sirois/Durham correct; "and a colleague" matches the two-author paper.

**Issue A. "Body-wide consequences" overstates a self-rated outcome** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "It reframes procrastination as a stress-generating trait with body-wide consequences rather than a time-management quirk"
- **Abstract says:** "chronic procrastination is associated with poor overall health status that can be explained in part by higher levels of stress" — the outcome throughout is self-rated health (SRH).
- **Problem:** "Stress-generating" implies a causal direction the cross-sectional design cannot support, and "body-wide consequences" implies measured physical health outcomes. The only outcome is a subjective health rating. The Caveats correctly note this, so the body text contradicts its own caveat.
- **Suggested fix:** "It reframes procrastination as a trait that travels with higher stress and poorer self-rated health, rather than being a mere time-management quirk — though the data cannot say which comes first."

**Issue B. NS fit score high for entirely self-reported cross-sectional data** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "**NS fit:** 7/10"
- **Problem:** Every input — procrastination, stress, current and future health — is self-reported, and every sample is cross-sectional. The large N pools the same design weakness 36 times. A 7 puts it level with Study 1, which rests on RCT biomarker data.
- **Suggested fix:** "**NS fit:** 6/10 — large multi-sample dataset on an everyday trait, but every measure is self-reported and every sample cross-sectional."

---

### Study 3: Newborn babies can already hear when their own language is spoken with a foreign rhythm
**PMID:** 42464912 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N = 44 Czech newborns, foreign-accented rhythm via prolonged foot-initial syllables, larger hemodynamic response to the foreign-rhythm version, right-lateralized — all accurate. The "traditional theories" framing matches the abstract closely.

**Issue A. "Single center" not stated in the abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "N = 44, single center"
- **Abstract says:** Author affiliations span Charles University (Prague and Hradec Králové) and Havlíčkův Brod Hospital; recruitment sites are not described.
- **Problem:** Unverifiable from abstract only, and the affiliation list suggests more than one site may have been involved.
- **Suggested fix:** "N = 44; recruitment site(s) not specified in the abstract"

**Issue B. NS fit 7/10 on N = 44** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "**NS fit:** 7/10 — overturns a textbook claim about what newborns can hear; clean design, but modest N and a single language pairing."
- **Problem:** The score is defensible on novelty and on the objectivity of the measure, but 44 infants, one language and one accent manipulation is thin ground for a 7 that rests on "overturns a textbook claim."
- **Suggested fix:** "**NS fit:** 6/10 — overturns a textbook claim, but on 44 infants and a single language/accent pairing, replication in another rhythm class is needed."

---

### Study 4: The evidence that therapy helps bullying victims largely vanishes once publication bias is corrected
**PMID:** 42658011 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

23 studies (CBT n = 15, imagery n = 8), g = 0.72 unadjusted pre-post internalizing, adjusted g = 0.26 and non-significant, self-perception/coping adjusted g = 0.98, follow-up internalizing g = 0.37 still significant, I² = 68–98% — all correct. Ghent/Koster correct.

**Issue A. Headline overstates the scope of what vanished** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "The evidence that therapy helps bullying victims largely vanishes once publication bias is corrected"
- **Abstract says:** "after adjusting for publication bias, the pre-post internalizing effect dropped to g = 0.26 and was no longer statistically significant. Conversely, the adjusted effect for self-perception and coping increased to g = 0.98, whereas the follow-up internalizing effect decreased (g = 0.37) but remained significant."
- **Problem:** Only one of three adjusted estimates lost significance. Another *increased* after adjustment and a third stayed significant. The headline claims a general collapse of the evidence base that the paper does not report; the body text correctly describes the split, so the headline is out of step with the entry it introduces.
- **Suggested fix:** "Correcting for publication bias flips which benefit of therapy for bullying victims looks strongest"

**Issue B. Internal inconsistency in the NS.com check** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "**NS.com check:** No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (1 hits)"
- **Problem:** The tick and the hit count contradict each other. If there is one hit, the prior-coverage check needs resolving before pitching.
- **Suggested fix:** Resolve the hit and restate: either "No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)" or "1 possible prior hit — check before pitching."

---

### Study 5: Brain stimulation for PTSD works on questionnaires but not on clinician interviews
**PMID:** 42680058 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

16 RCTs, 786 participants in the primary sham comparison, significant large effect on self-reported symptoms, non-significant interview-based outcomes, wide prediction intervals, sparse follow-up evidence, mild adverse events, low-to-very-low certainty — all accurate. Peñate-Castro / University of La Laguna correct.

**Issue A. "Clinician" interviews not specified** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "not on clinician interviews" / "trained assessors can't detect it"
- **Abstract says:** "Findings based on interview-reported outcomes did not reach statistical significance."
- **Problem:** The abstract says "interview-reported," not who conducted the interviews or whether raters were blinded. The digest's NS fit line goes further still ("blinded-rater outcomes"). Unverifiable from abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "not on interview-based measures" — and in the NS fit note, "a clean split between self-report and interview-based outcomes."

**NS fit 6/10:** Defensible.

---

### Study 6: Men recover from PTSD in about a decade — for women it takes twice as long
**PMID:** 42303590 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

n = 15,893, lifetime prevalence 7.1%, projected lifetime risk 9.6%, OR 2.3 for females, projected lifetime remission 63.3%, three-quarters remitting by 10 years (males) versus 20 years (females), no change since 2007, and the comorbidity odds cited in the wider angle (asthma 2.0, diabetes 1.8, sedative use disorder 7.9) all match. Mills/Matilda Centre correct.

**Issue A. Headline generalizes a 75th-percentile figure into typical recovery** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Men recover from PTSD in about a decade — for women it takes twice as long"
- **Abstract says:** "Projected lifetime remission was 63.3% ... Three quarters entered remission after 10 years for males and 20 years for females."
- **Problem:** The 10/20-year figures are the point at which three quarters of those who ever remit have done so — not an average recovery time — and only about 63% remit at all. The headline reads as though everyone recovers, on that timetable.
- **Suggested fix:** "Three-quarters of men with PTSD remit within a decade — for women it takes twenty years"

**NS fit 6/10:** Defensible for nationally representative diagnostic-interview data.

---

### Study 7: On days you procrastinate, tomorrow's stress rises — and stress feeds back into attention problems
**PMID:** 42695429 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. N = 187, mean age 19.7, 78% women, 28 days of EMA, temporal/contemporaneous/between-subject networks, the two directional findings (concentration difficulties and procrastination → next-day stress; stress, especially lacking control → next-day ADHD symptoms), and the contemporaneous prominence of procrastination, restlessness and concentration difficulties all match the abstract. Framing is appropriately correlational and the Caveats flag the non-clinical sample, self-report and network-model limits. Goh / University of Hawai'i at Mānoa correct.

---

### Study 8: Difficulty naming your own emotions seems to protect fragile narcissists from burnout
**PMID:** 42700715 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N = 1,239, Swiss inpatient clinic, April 2018–November 2024, alexithymia/ERI/overcommitment as predictors, and the significant negative alexithymia × narcissistic vulnerability interaction (b = −0.207, p = .016) with attenuation at high alexithymia — all accurate. Ledermann / University Hospital Zurich correct.

**Issue A. Omits that narcissistic vulnerability itself was only a trend** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Unexpectedly, the alexithymia × narcissistic vulnerability interaction was significant and negative: at high levels of alexithymia, the effect of narcissistic vulnerability on burnout was attenuated."
- **Abstract says:** "Narcissistic vulnerability showed a trend toward significance (b = 0.124, p = .062). The alexithymia × narcissism interaction was significant (b = −0.207, p = .016)."
- **Problem:** The main effect being buffered did not itself reach significance. A headline built on "protects fragile narcissists from burnout" implies an established harm that alexithymia then blunts; the paper reports a non-significant main effect and a significant interaction, which is a much weaker foundation. A reader — or an editor — would assume more.
- **Suggested fix:** Add to the study description: "Narcissistic vulnerability alone only trended toward predicting burnout (p = .062), so the buffering interaction is modifying an effect that was not itself statistically significant."

**Issue B. "Single strongest predictor" claim on unstandardized coefficients** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "effort–reward imbalance remains the single strongest predictor in this dataset"
- **Abstract says:** "Burnout was significantly predicted by alexithymia (b = 0.241, p < .001), ERI quotient (b = 0.431, p < .001), overcommitment (b = 0.063, p < .001), psychological distress (b = 0.025, p = .004), and age (b = −0.014, p < .001)."
- **Problem:** These are unstandardized coefficients on differently scaled measures; they cannot be ranked directly. ERI has the largest b, but "strongest predictor" isn't established.
- **Suggested fix:** "effort–reward imbalance at work was one of the strongest predictors reported"

**NS fit 5/10:** Defensible.

---

### Study 9: Loneliness predicts later suicidal thoughts even after accounting for depression and anxiety
**PMID:** 42642073 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N = 4,277, ages 18–89, two waves, four age groups, covariates (gender, social circle, depression, anxiety, stress, prior lifetime suicidality), and 25.2–39.3% variance explained all match. Teismann / Ruhr-Universität Bochum correct. Framing is appropriately prospective-associational and the pitch explicitly says "risk assessment research, not a treatment claim."

**Issue A. "Across all four age bands" is an inference** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Across all four age bands, loneliness remained a significant predictor after controlling for..."
- **Abstract says:** "three-step hierarchical regression analyses were conducted in each age group, respectively ... Loneliness proved to be significantly associated with T1-suicidal ideation and/or behaviour, beyond affective symptoms, social circle and previous suicidal ideation and/or behaviour."
- **Problem:** The abstract reports the analyses were run per age group and reports the overall conclusion, but does not state that the association was significant in every one of the four groups. Unverifiable from abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "Loneliness remained a significant predictor after controlling for gender, size of social circle, depression, anxiety, stress and prior lifetime suicidality; analyses were run separately in four age bands (check with the authors whether it held in each)."

**NS fit 5/10:** Defensible.

---

### Study 10: Living with long-term stress may blunt, not amplify, the daily link between hassles and low mood
**PMID:** 42595230 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. N = 61 YMSM living with HIV, three US Adolescent Trial Network sites, 66 days of phone-based daily assessment, baseline chronic HIV stressors, daily stressors associated with both higher level (b = 0.45) and greater intraindividual variability (b = 0.42) of depressed mood, and attenuation rather than amplification by chronic HIV stressors — all match. The "Why it matters" mirrors the authors' own two candidate explanations (dysregulation versus adaptiveness of some adversity), the headline is hedged with "may," and the Caveats flag the N, the specificity of the population and the possibility of reporting artefacts.

---

### Study 11: Erratic dinner times are linked to more depressive symptoms — breakfast and lunch aren't
**PMID:** 42624213 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

450 adults aged 20–59, Tehran, three non-consecutive 24-h recalls, composite phase deviation scores, dinner irregularity B = 1.08 for depressive symptoms, nulls for breakfast, lunch, anxiety and stress, and the null tertile analysis (correctly placed in Caveats) all check out. Shab-Bidar / Tehran University of Medical Sciences correct, and the pitch responsibly warns against implying treatment.

**Issue A. Analytic N for the key finding is 404, not 450** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "assessed 450 healthy adults aged 20–59 using three non-consecutive 24-hour dietary recalls"
- **Abstract says:** "This cross-sectional study included 450 apparently healthy adults ... Linear regression analyses included participants with complete data for all model variables (n = 404)."
- **Problem:** The B = 1.08 result the entry is built on comes from the 404-person complete-case linear models, not the full 450. Small but worth stating in a pitch.
- **Suggested fix:** "assessed 450 healthy adults aged 20–59 ... with the linear models run on the 404 participants with complete data"

**Issue B. Circadian-anchor mechanism asserted beyond the data** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "then explain why the evening meal may be the body clock's most important non-light cue"
- **Abstract says:** "Dinner timing irregularity may be associated with higher depressive symptom scores in this sample ... Future prospective and intervention studies are needed to clarify temporality and underlying mechanisms."
- **Problem:** The study tested no circadian mechanism and made no claim about the relative strength of meal timing as a zeitgeber. The hedge "may" softens it, but the pitch presents it as the explanation for the finding.
- **Suggested fix:** "then explore the chrononutrition hypothesis that meal timing acts as a non-light cue for the body clock — a mechanism this study did not test"

**NS fit 5/10:** Defensible.

---

### Study 12: Children born preterm run hot: raised heart rate at five, but normal stress regulation
**PMID:** 42693548 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

70 preterm children aged 5.5 versus 32 matched full-term controls, 98% White, greater social difficulties and internalizing problems, consistently elevated heart rate, comparable HRV, conversation tasks eliciting strongest autonomic activation — all accurate. Boets / KU Leuven correct, and the "hyperarousal not impaired regulation" framing matches the authors' own conclusion.

**Issue A. "Exactly the same way" overstates "comparable"** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "their heart rate variability tracked social context in exactly the same way as full-term peers"
- **Abstract says:** "HRV patterns were comparable with the full-term group ... Across both groups, RMSSD-HRV varied by interaction partner ... while HF-HRV reflected general condition effects independent of partner familiarity."
- **Problem:** "Comparable" is not equivalence; the study was not powered as an equivalence test, and "exactly the same" invites readers to treat a null difference as proof of identical regulation.
- **Suggested fix:** "their heart rate variability tracked social context in much the same way as full-term peers"

**Issue B. "Parent-reported social difficulties" not specified in abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "parent-reported social difficulties"
- **Abstract says:** "Preterm children demonstrated significantly greater social difficulties and internalizing problems than full-term peers" — the source of these ratings is not stated.
- **Problem:** Unverifiable from abstract only. Same applies to "single center," though the UZ Leuven affiliation makes it plausible.
- **Suggested fix:** "social and internalising difficulties (measurement source not specified in the abstract — confirm with the authors)"

**NS fit 5/10:** Defensible.

---

### Study 13: When childhood abuse happens may matter more than how much of it there was
**PMID:** 42683544 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. N = 116, 30.5% women, mean age 26.3, formerly residentially placed, MACE-X timing and type data, blood-based oxidative stress markers, adolescent abuse associated with higher GRed and neglect with lower, neglect at ages 8 and 12 highest variable importance for GPx/GRed, and the null for overall severity, multiplicity and duration — all match. Clemens (Ulm) and Bürgin (Basel) correctly placed. The pitch's instruction to "frame strictly as biomarker association, not risk prediction" is exactly right for exploratory random-forest data, and the ACE-score angle is presented as editorial context rather than a study claim.

---

### Study 14: Children whose parents and coaches both push winning report the most stress — and the least fun
**PMID:** 42419608 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N = 347, 64.6% female (rounded to 65%), mean age 12.5, five latent profiles, mastery-dominant profiles reporting adaptive outcomes and performance-leaning profiles maladaptive ones, and the dual mastery-and-performance profile reporting both simultaneously — all accurate. Fuller and Moore / East Carolina University correct, and the Caveats correctly rule out causal reading.

**Issue A. Headline superlative not supported** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Children whose parents and coaches both push winning report the most stress — and the least fun"
- **Abstract says:** "When athletes perceived climates that were predominately performance-involving, they reported more maladaptive outcomes (e.g., ego orientations, low enjoyment, high stress)."
- **Problem:** The abstract reports directional group differences, not a ranking establishing that this profile scored highest on stress and lowest on enjoyment of all five. "Most" and "least" are superlatives the abstract doesn't license — and the more interesting finding the entry itself leads with is the *dual* profile.
- **Suggested fix:** "Children whose parents and coaches both push winning report more stress — and less fun"

**NS fit 5/10:** Defensible.

---

### Study 15: Growing up in a war zone changes which brain circuits track a child's attachment style
**PMID:** 42607893 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. N = 79 (42 war-exposed, 37 non-exposed), resting-state fMRI, parent-reported EF, no group differences in attachment and no EF difference after adjustment for scan timing and nonverbal ability, and the divergent coupling (cingulate–amygdala in war-exposed, amygdala–hippocampal in non-exposed) all match. Horowitz-Kraus / Technion correct. The Caveats correctly reproduce the authors' own flag that the large-scale network simple slopes did not survive correction for multiple comparisons, and the pitch instructs the writer to "emphasize preliminary status" — consistent with the abstract's "preliminary evidence" language. The "Why it matters" avoids causal claims, matching the authors' call for longitudinal work.

---

### Study 16: The largest genetic map yet of everyday moodiness and impulsivity points to two different brain regions
**PMID:** 42679763 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

13 GWAS, n = 64,000–1,200,000, 184 EXT and 31 INT loci, 70 novel genes (52 + 18), hippocampal CA4 for EXT and amygdalar excitatory neurons for INT, and the independent PRS cohort of 4,565 all match. Franke / Radboud correct, and the Medice disclosure is properly carried into the Caveats.

**Issue A. "Largest genetic map yet" is not claimed by the authors** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "The largest genetic map yet of everyday moodiness and impulsivity"
- **Abstract says:** No priority or size claim is made; the paper describes "a multivariate framework to population-based, non-clinical traits."
- **Problem:** Unverifiable from abstract only, and superlatives of this kind are the first thing an editor will ask you to source.
- **Suggested fix:** "A large genetic map of everyday moodiness and impulsivity points to two different brain regions"

**Issue B. Genetic correlation described as shared variants with a behavioral effect** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "the same variants that make someone restless in the general population are the ones enriched in ADHD and substance-use disorder"
- **Abstract says:** "EXT correlated with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder and substance-use disorders" (via LD score regression).
- **Problem:** Two errors in one clause. First, "make someone restless" is causal language for GWAS association data. Second, a genome-wide genetic correlation is not a statement that specific identified variants are "enriched in" a diagnosis; it is an aggregate statistic about shared genetic architecture.
- **Suggested fix:** "the genetic variation associated with externalizing traits in the general population overlaps substantially with the genetic architecture of ADHD and substance-use disorders"

**Issue C. "Predicted" for a polygenic score association** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "internalizing polygenic scores predicted emotional well-being in an independent cohort of 4,565 people"
- **Abstract says:** "PRS-CS demonstrated association of INT liability with emotional well-being."
- **Problem:** "Predicted" implies useful individual-level prediction — which the digest's own Caveats correctly deny ("effect sizes at the individual level are tiny and non-predictive"). The body contradicts the caveat.
- **Suggested fix:** "internalizing polygenic scores were associated with emotional well-being in an independent cohort of 4,565 people"

**NS fit 5/10:** Defensible.

---

### Study 17: Older men with more mentally rich lifestyles report less stress — but more loneliness
**PMID:** 42687444 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N = 80 (33 men), ages 65–101, DASS-21/SWLS/UCLA/CRS, the male-only association of higher CRS with lower perceived stress and greater loneliness, associations with selected attention measures but not memory span, and the authors' own caution about sex-specific findings all match. The Caveats and the "Not much yet" framing in "Why it matters" are appropriately restrained.

**Issue A. Contact attributed to the wrong institution** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Call Mikhail Ordin at the University of the Basque Country"
- **Abstract says:** Ordin's affiliations are "Faculdade de Medicina, Universidade de Coimbra" and "Interdisciplinary Centre for European Sudies, Europa Universität Flensburg." The University of the Basque Country is the affiliation of the fourth author, Polyanskaya.
- **Problem:** A writer following the digest would approach the wrong institution's press office.
- **Suggested fix:** "Call Mikhail Ordin at the University of Coimbra (or Leona Polyanskaya at the University of the Basque Country)"

**Issue B. Cognitive reserve measure described more broadly than the authors do** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "measures of cognitive reserve (built from educational, occupational and leisure engagement)"
- **Abstract says:** "The CRS was used as a proxy measure of the leisure-activity contribution to cognitive reserve rather than as a comprehensive or direct measure of cognitive reserve."
- **Problem:** The authors explicitly narrow what the CRS captures here. The digest's own wider angle notes "how thin the evidence for the leisure component" is, so the body text is at odds with its own angle.
- **Suggested fix:** "measures of cognitive reserve — used by the authors specifically as a proxy for the leisure-activity component of reserve, not a comprehensive measure"

**NS fit 4/10:** Defensible, and correctly justified in the note.

### Study 18: A key theory of what drives suicidal thinking holds up in the US but not in the UK
**PMID:** 42683538 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

Sample sizes (US college n = 865; UK community n = 734), the defeat/entrapment–ideation associations in both samples, higher lifetime ideation among SGM participants in both, and the moderation appearing only in Sample 1 and only for entrapment, are all accurately reported in the body. O'Connor as IMV originator is correct.

**Issue A. Headline reverses what actually failed to replicate** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "A key theory of what drives suicidal thinking holds up in the US but not in the UK"
- **Abstract says:** "Defeat and entrapment were significantly associated with suicide ideation in both samples. In Sample 1, SGM status moderated the association between entrapment and suicide ideation ... In Sample 2, no moderation effects of SGM status were found."
- **Problem:** The IMV model's core prediction held in *both* countries. What did not replicate is a single moderation effect involving SGM status. As written the headline tells a reader the theory failed in the UK, which is the opposite of what the paper found — and the digest's own NS fit note concedes "the main effects replicate fine."
- **Suggested fix:** "A suicide theory's core holds in both the US and UK — but the minority-stress twist only shows up in one"

**Issue B. "Predicted" for cross-sectional associations** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Defeat and entrapment predicted suicidal ideation in both samples"
- **Abstract says:** "Defeat and entrapment were significantly associated with suicide ideation in both samples."
- **Problem:** "Predicted" implies temporal ordering the design does not provide; the Caveats correctly note the study is cross-sectional and ideation is measured retrospectively.
- **Suggested fix:** "Defeat and entrapment were associated with suicidal ideation in both samples"

**NS fit 4/10:** Defensible.

### Study 19: Nonbinary people describe the current political climate in the language of trauma and bereavement
**PMID:** 42658624 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

Mixed methods, thematic analysis of write-in survey responses, chi-square tests by race, gender expression and geography, the four themes, and both subgroup findings (rural → loss of authenticity; gender-nonconforming → loss of potential future) are all accurate. Matsuno / Arizona State correct, and the Caveats correctly flag the absence of clinical outcome measures.

**Issue A. "Assess and code" implies clinical guidance the study cannot give** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "a framing with direct implications for how clinicians assess and code such distress"
- **Abstract says:** "Findings from this study present further conceptualizations of sociopolitical trauma and stress among the TNB community."
- **Problem:** "Code" points at diagnostic coding. This is a qualitative thematic analysis with no diagnostic instruments, no comparison group and no clinical outcomes; it cannot support implications for clinical assessment or coding practice. The digest's own Caveats say "no clinical outcome measures."
- **Suggested fix:** "a framing that could change how clinicians and researchers conceptualise this kind of distress"

**NS fit 4/10:** Defensible, and correctly justified by the qualitative design.
